rv.q: Close's return to the role that made her a Broadway legend is nothing short of triumphant, a master class in musical theater acting that reminds you why she owned this part in the first place.
Close's performance is so ferociously committed that it's impossible to look away, even when you want to.

The lush orchestrations do ample justice to the beauty of Lloyd Webber's score, which includes the aforementioned "As If We Never Said Goodbye" and "With One Look," two songs that went on to become standards.
The audacity of this performance is matched by its veracity.
Her experience, knowledge and craft prove that Sunset Boulevard is an old warhorse that can still finish the race in first place.
Like the merchandise, the show is a limited edition selling paste and glitter as treasures.
Ms. Close's performance is a tour de force of theatrical artifice, but the production around her feels oddly cramped and underpowered

The show's atmosphere is at once messy and banal; its relentless pop façade and the constant drama of its music preclude intimacy and distance us from feeling, while encouraging a kind of aggressive contempt.
Her masterful portrayal also delivers the one thing poor nutty Norma most craves: An adoring, utterly captivated audience, and applause that echoes long after the curtain falls.
Her presence resulted in a magical moment.
The moment is as good as musical-theater gets.

Director Lonny Price and his lead actress seem determined to force you out of the moment, overloading the production with so many "Major Theatrical Event" moments and signposts that it all starts to sag beneath the weight of its own self-importance.
Maybe this was a great story on film; I didn’t get it on stage.

cn.t: Critics praise Glenn Close's masterful return as Norma Desmond, but many find the scaled-down production underwhelming compared to her commanding performance, resulting in mixed reception for this Lloyd Webber revival.
